opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things our team spends a lot of energy on. Every time a major new model drops, there's this race, right? Developers want to try it immediately, and they want it to be fast, reliable, and affordable from day one. So we think about it in a few layers.

The first layer is just getting it running correctly. New models often come with architectural twists: a different attention variant, a new mixture-of-experts routing scheme, longer context windows, new tokenizers, multimodal inputs. Each of those can touch our serving stack in different places. So the initial work is making sure we faithfully reproduce the model's quality. That sounds basic, but it's surprisingly easy to get subtle numerical differences, especially when you start applying optimizations, so we invest heavily in evaluation to make sure what we serve matches the reference behavior.

The second layer is performance. Out of the box, a new architecture usually isn't optimized. That's where a lot of our engineering goes: custom kernels, quantization that preserves quality, speculative decoding, smart batching, caching, and figuring out the right hardware configuration and how to shard the model across GPUs. Mixture-of-experts models in particular have very different memory and communication patterns than dense models, so the optimal deployment can look quite different.

The third layer is making it production-grade. That means things like function calling, structured output, consistent APIs, scaling up and down with traffic, and reliability guarantees. Enterprises don't just want to play with a model; they want to build products on it.

What's helped us over time is building our stack so it's modular and composable. When a new model comes out, we're not starting from scratch. We can reuse a lot of the building blocks and focus on what's genuinely new. That's how we've been able to support many of the big open models on day zero or within days of release.

And longer term, we see the model release cadence only accelerating. So the real investment isn't any single model; it's the infrastructure and automation that make onboarding the next one faster, and then letting developers customize and tune those models for their own use cases on top of that.

r001.rationale: The response says the platform aims to support models on day zero or within days, and separately describes production features, but does not say model availability precedes rollout of surrounding functionality.

r002.rationale: It mentions longer context windows as an architectural change, but does not explain that they increase the computational burden of processing tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, great to be here.

So the way I think about it is that supporting a new model is really two different problems, and people tend to conflate them. The first is just getting the model to run correctly. The second is getting it to run fast and cheap enough that it's actually useful in production. The first one is table stakes, the second one is where all the real work is.

On the first part, there's been a lot of convergence. Most of the open models coming out today, whether it's Llama, Mixtral, Qwen, DeepSeek, they share a lot of architectural DNA. Attention, MLP blocks, some variation on RoPE, maybe mixture of experts. So when a new model drops, often it's a matter of mapping the config, making sure the tokenizer is handled correctly, checking the chat template, and validating numerics against the reference implementation. We've invested a lot in making that path boring. Our goal is that a new model in a known family should be up within hours, not days.

But every few months something genuinely new shows up. Multi-head latent attention in DeepSeek is a good example. Or a new quantization format, or a different approach to long context. Those break assumptions in the inference stack, and that's where you have to go back to the kernels. That's really the heart of what we do. We write our own CUDA kernels, we have our own serving stack, and the reason we do that is precisely so we're not waiting on upstream frameworks to catch up when a model introduces something novel.

The other thing I'd say is that "support" doesn't end when the model is live. The first version we ship is almost never the fastest version. There's a whole tail of work after launch: speculative decoding tuned for that model, figuring out the right quantization that preserves quality, batching strategies for the traffic patterns we actually see, and so on. For the popular models that tail can go on for months, and each pass meaningfully changes the cost per token.

And honestly, the thing that gates all of this is evaluation. Speed is useless if quality regressed. So a lot of our effort is building the harness that lets us say with confidence that a quantized, optimized version of a model behaves the same as the reference. Customers won't tolerate surprises there, and they shouldn't.

So the short version is: the day-one work is mostly solved, the hard work is the long tail of making it genuinely production grade, and owning the full stack is what lets us move fast on both.

r001.rationale: The response says basic model support can arrive within hours and optimization continues after launch, but it does not describe surrounding platform functionality rolling out later.

r002.rationale: It mentions long-context approaches as a possible source of inference-stack changes, but does not explain that longer context windows increase the computational burden of processing tokens.

astra-6.text:
We think about it as an ongoing engineering effort. A new model comes out, and getting it to load and produce a response is only the first step. To support it well, you need to understand its architecture, where the bottlenecks are, and how it behaves under real production traffic. Then you have to make it efficient and reliable.

Some models fit into the infrastructure you already have, so support can happen very quickly. Others introduce something new that requires deeper work across the inference stack. The goal is to absorb that complexity for developers, so they can try a new model and decide whether it improves their application without having to rebuild the serving infrastructure themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says some models can be supported quickly and others require deeper inference-stack work, but does not state that model availability on release day comes before rollout of surrounding platform functionality.

r002.rationale: It mentions understanding model architecture, bottlenecks, and production behavior, but does not explain that longer context windows increase the computational burden of processing tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
The model landscape is moving so fast that supporting a new model can’t be a one-off engineering project every time. We think about it in layers: can we get the model running correctly, can we make it run efficiently, and can we make it reliable in production?

Getting it to run is just the beginning. You have to understand its architecture, its memory requirements, and how it behaves under different workloads. Then there’s the optimization work—how you batch requests, how you use the GPUs, and how you balance latency and throughput. Those decisions can be different from one model to another.

So the investment is really in building a platform where as much of that work as possible is reusable. When a new model comes out, we want to focus on what’s actually new about it, and let the platform handle the common pieces. That’s how you keep up with the pace of releases while still giving people something they can depend on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making model support reusable and reliable, but does not say that models become available on release day before surrounding platform functionality rolls out.

r002.rationale: The response mentions memory requirements and workload optimization, but does not connect longer context windows to increased computational burden when processing tokens.
